## Introduction
This module develops the foundational skill of observation as the spark for scientific inquiry. It emphasises designing and conducting simple observations, distinguishing observations from inferences, and using initial primary data to plan further investigations. It also prompts students to recognise the role of observation in historical science and in Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples’ knowledge of Country/Place. For course framing, see the official NESA syllabus overview and Year 11 module list. ([educationstandards.nsw.edu.au](https://www.educationstandards.nsw.edu.au/wps/portal/nesa/11-12/stage-6-learning-areas/stage-6-science/investigating-science-2017?utm_source=openai), [nsw.gov.au](https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/investigating-science-stage-6-2017?utm_source=openai))

## Inquiry Question 1 – How does observation instigate scientific investigation?
### Concepts
- Carry out a practical investigation to record both quantitative and qualitative data from observations.
- Discuss and evaluate the characteristics of observations made compared with inferences drawn from the practical investigation.
- Research how observation has instigated experimentation to investigate cause and effect in historical examples.
- Assess ways in which Aboriginal and Torres Strait Islander Peoples use observation to understand Country and Place and to manage the natural environment.

## Question Bank
### Multiple-Choice (answers hidden in collapsible blocks)
1. Q: In this module, what distinguishes an observation from an inference?
- A. Observations are conclusions drawn from data; inferences are raw measurements
- B. Observations are direct records from senses/devices; inferences interpret what those records might mean
- C. Observations must be numerical; inferences must be descriptive
- D. Observations are always accurate; inferences are always uncertain
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. Observations are direct qualitative/quantitative records; inferences are interpretations based on those records (as emphasised across IQ1–IQ2).</details>

2. Q: Which action best shows how primary data can prompt further investigation?
- A. Rewriting the hypothesis to match expected results
- B. Using initial measurements to design a refined method targeting a new variable
- C. Comparing your results with a textbook diagram
- D. Stopping once any data have been collected
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. IQ3 and IQ5 highlight using gathered primary data to plan refined methods and identify next questions.</details>

### Short-Answer / Calculation
1. Q: Give one example of a qualitative observation and one of a quantitative observation from the same practical.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Qualitative: colour change observed in a solution. Quantitative: temperature recorded as 22.4 °C. Drawn from IQ2 focus on both forms.</details>

2. Q: Explain one way observational tools can limit conclusions in an investigation.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Tools determine resolution, range and precision; limitations (e.g., scale with 1 g graduations) constrain the sensitivity and therefore the strength of conclusions. From IQ3.</details>

## Question Bank
### Multiple-Choice
1. Q: Which action best validates an inference made from primary data?
- A. Repeating the inference to the class
- B. Searching for secondary-sourced data that support or challenge it
- C. Changing units to make the trend look stronger
- D. Ignoring outliers to improve the correlation
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. IQ2 centres on using secondary sources to test inferences from primary data.</details>

2. Q: An “outlier” in a dataset is best described as:
- A. Any datum that reduces the correlation coefficient
- B. An observation markedly distant from the rest, warranting investigation before deciding how to treat it
- C. A measurement error that must always be deleted
- D. A result proving the hypothesis false
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. It is a markedly different observation; investigate before removal or use robust methods. ([itl.nist.gov](https://itl.nist.gov/div898/handbook/eda/section3/eda35h.htm?utm_source=openai))</details>

### Short-Answer
1. Q: Explain how pattern-recognition can mislead scientists and how to counter this risk.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Humans tend to see patterns even in randomness, which can produce spurious hypotheses. Counter by pre-registering methods, using appropriate statistics, testing with new data, and consulting secondary sources (IQ2–IQ3).</details>

2. Q: Outline one way peers improve the quality of an investigation.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Peers provide alternative perspectives that can reveal biases, refine hypotheses, and challenge assumptions (IQ6).</details>

## Question Bank
### Multiple-Choice
1. Q: A scientific model is best described as:
- A. A perfect replica of reality
- B. A representation used to explain, predict, or explore aspects of a system under simplifying assumptions
- C. A hypothesis that has been proven
- D. A law expressed mathematically
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. Models are representational tools with assumptions and limits. ([plato.stanford.edu](https://plato.stanford.edu/entries/models-science/?utm_source=openai))</details>

2. Q: When new evidence conflicts with a widely used model, scientists should:
- A. Ignore the evidence to preserve consensus
- B. Immediately discard the model without analysis
- C. Reassess assumptions, refine or replace the model as needed
- D. Treat the evidence as an outlier
<details><summary>Answer</summary>C. IQ3 focuses on revision of models in light of evidence.</details>

### Short-Answer
1. Q: Give one benefit and one limitation of using a simple model over a complex one.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Benefit: clarity and accessibility for explanation. Limitation: may omit critical variables, reducing accuracy (IQ3).</details>

2. Q: Describe a phenomenon you could model and state what data would refine your model.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Example: modelling cooling of a hot object; refine with time–temperature data at different environments (IQ4).</details>

## Question Bank
### Multiple-Choice
1. Q: A scientific law primarily:
- A. Explains why phenomena occur
- B. Describes consistent relationships under specified conditions, often mathematically
- C. Is a speculative idea awaiting evidence
- D. Is replaced once a theory is formed
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. Laws describe regularities; theories offer explanatory frameworks.</details>

2. Q: Which activity best supports the development of a theory?
- A. Collecting a single anecdote
- B. Gathering convergent evidence from multiple, independent sources over time
- C. Rewording a law
- D. Relying on expert opinion alone
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. IQ2 emphasises sustained evidential support.</details>

### Short-Answer
1. Q: In a conservation-of-mass practical, the measured mass decreases after a reaction. Give one plausible methodological cause.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Gas escape from an unsealed system (methodological limitation), not a violation of the law.</details>

2. Q: Briefly differentiate “theory” and “law” using plate tectonics and conservation of mass as anchors.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Plate tectonics is a theory that explains mechanisms of continental movement; conservation of mass is a law describing a consistent quantitative relationship in closed systems.</details>

## Introduction
This module develops full-cycle investigation competence: identifying triggers for inquiry, selecting and justifying methodology, executing and evaluating investigations (validity, reliability), and reporting scientifically. It aligns with planning/conducting outcomes and with conventions for scientific communication. ([nsw.gov.au](https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/investigating-science-stage-6-2017?utm_source=openai))

## Inquiry Question 1 – What initiates an investigation?
### Concepts
- Research factors that led scientists to investigate phenomena (e.g., observation → question → hypothesis).
- Case study – Microwaves (Percy Spencer): accidental melting of a chocolate bar near radar led to tests (e.g., popcorn) and ultimately the microwave oven.
- Propose reasons for scientists’ investigations by examining the types of data they sought.
- Determine hypotheses tested in each investigation.
- Describe where deviations from traditional/linear methodologies were needed to test each hypothesis.

## Inquiry Question 3 – How is the integrity of a scientific investigation judged?
### Concepts
- Evaluate the design of the student investigation.
- Conduct the planned investigation; collect, record and analyse primary data.
- Draw conclusions and suggest further investigation or research.
- Evaluate the validity of the investigation.
- Evaluate the reliability of the investigation.

### Definitions (from graph)
- Validity: “An experiment is valid if its method is appropriate and directly tests the intended hypothesis. Core components include controlling variables, having a single independent variable, and appropriate measurement of the dependent variable.” HSC example: 2021 Q22b GMO mice x diet groups illustrate control/IV structure.
- Reliability: “An experiment is reliable if the results are consistent and repeatable. This is achieved through repetition (at least 3 trials) and using a sufficiently large sample size.” HSC example: 2020 Q25a self-injection—unreliable with n=1.

## Inquiry Question 4 – What is the structure of an investigative report?
### Concepts
- Review a published, peer‑reviewed scientific report to determine conventions of writing (structure, style).
- Identify purpose, language style, presentation and structure using a secondary source sample.
- Compare structures/functions of a scientific investigation and its written report.
- Prepare a report on the student investigation.

### Definitions (from graph)
- Scientific report conventions: “Aim, Hypothesis, Method, Results, Discussion, Conclusion; objective third-person language with precise scientific terminology.” HSC example: 2023 Q30—penalised for informal headings/colloquial terms.

## Glossary of Key Terms
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Validity | An experiment directly tests the intended hypothesis; control of variables; single IV; appropriate DV measurement. |
| Reliability | Results are consistent/repeatable; repetition (≥3 trials) and adequate sample size. |
| Scientific report (structure/style) | Aim, Hypothesis, Method, Results, Discussion, Conclusion; objective third-person language, precise terminology. |

## Question Bank
### Multiple-Choice
1. Q: Which change most directly improves validity?
- A. Increasing trials from 1 to 3
- B. Adding a second independent variable
- C. Introducing a control while holding all variables constant except the IV
- D. Using informal language in the report
<details><summary>Answer</summary>C. Validity is about method appropriateness and isolating the IV with controls.</details>

2. Q: A study with n=1 and no repeats primarily fails on:
- A. Accuracy
- B. Reliability
- C. Validity
- D. Ethics
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. Reliability—consistency/replicability needs repeats/sample size.</details>

### Short-Answer
1. Q: State two features of a scientifically written report that would be penalised if missing.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Correct sectioning (e.g., Hypothesis, Method) and objective, precise terminology (avoid colloquialisms) per the definition/HSC example.</details>

2. Q: Distinguish a design flaw affecting validity from one affecting reliability in the same investigation.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Validity flaw: two independent variables changed simultaneously. Reliability flaw: only one trial per condition (no replication).</details>

## Introduction
Students examine how measurement technologies shape data quality (accuracy, error, safety) and how science and technology co‑evolve: new tools enable discoveries that, in turn, drive further technologies. ([nsw.gov.au](https://www.nsw.gov.au/education-and-training/nesa/curriculum/science/investigating-science-stage-6-2017?utm_source=openai))

## Inquiry Question 1 – How does technology enhance and/or limit scientific investigation?
### Concepts
- Design a practical using available technologies to measure IV and DV and produce quantitative data.
- Conduct the investigation; evaluate limitations of the technologies used.
- Investigate measuring devices used; assess likelihood of random/systematic errors and degree of accuracy.
- Compare accuracy of analogue and digital technologies in making observations.
- Assess safety of selected technologies using chemical safety data and WHS guidelines. ## Question Bank
### Multiple-Choice
1. Q: A digital sensor with known calibration drift primarily risks:
- A. Reduced validity only
- B. Systematic error (bias) affecting accuracy
- C. Random error only
- D. Ethical non-compliance by default
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. Drift introduces systematic error, biasing measurements.</details>

2. Q: In the glow‑stick practical, placing one stick in hot water and one in ice shows that:
- A. Higher temperature slows the reaction but brightens light
- B. Higher temperature accelerates the reaction, increasing brightness but shortening duration
- C. Lower temperature increases both brightness and duration
- D. Temperature has no effect
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. Reaction rate rises with temperature, increasing brightness but reducing duration. ([acs.org](https://www.acs.org/education/celebrating-chemistry-editions/2021-ncw/slow-the-glow.html?utm_source=openai))</details>

### Short-Answer
1. Q: Give one advantage and one limitation of an analogue device compared with its digital counterpart.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Advantage: may offer continuous readout that reveals trends. Limitation: harder to read precisely (parallax), increasing random error.</details>

2. Q: Identify one WHS step you must take before using a new chemical reagent in a school experiment.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Obtain and consult the current Safety Data Sheet and complete a risk assessment in line with NSW guidance. ([education.nsw.gov.au](https://education.nsw.gov.au/teaching-and-learning/curriculum/science/science-safety-and-compliance?utm_source=openai), [safework.nsw.gov.au](https://www.safework.nsw.gov.au/hazards-a-z/hazardous-chemical/general-requirements/general-requirements-accordion/obtain-and-provide-safety-information?utm_source=openai))</details>

## Inquiry Question 3 – What type of evidence is needed to draw valid conclusions?
### Concepts
- Evaluate how evidence of a correlation can be misinterpreted as causation.

### Definitions (from graph)
- Correlation vs causation: correlation = variables change together; causation = one variable directly causes change in another; confusing the two is a fallacy. HSC example: 2019 Q25c whales vs CO₂.

### Case Studies
- The Hawthorne Effect: observation itself influences results (workers’ productivity increases when observed).

### Practical Examples
- (not mentioned)

### Links to Outcomes
- INS12-14 — Uses evidence-based analysis to support or refute a hypothesis.

### Exam Alignment (no full question text)

## Inquiry Question 4 – How does the reporting of science influence the general public's understanding of the subject?
### Concepts
- Examine a contemporary scientific debate and its portrayal in mainstream media.
- Evaluate use/interpretation of “theory”, “hypothesis”, “belief”, “law” in media reporting.
- Compare reporting between a peer‑reviewed journal article and popular media.
- Analyse how conflicts of interest can suppress, misinterpret or misrepresent evidence.
- Describe the halo effect; explain how positive perceptions can reject valid alternatives.
- Analyse a pseudo‑scientific claim and how scientific language/processes are manipulated to sway opinion.

### Definitions (from graph)
- Pseudoscience: claim/belief/practice presented as scientific but not adhering to the scientific method; often uses scientific‑sounding language to mislead. HSC example: 2020 Q27a astrology.

- (not mentioned)

### Links to Outcomes

## Glossary of Key Terms
| Term | Definition |
|------|------------|
| Correlation vs causation | Correlation: variables change together; causation: one directly produces change in the other; conflating them is a fallacy. |
| Pseudoscience | A claim presented as scientific without adhering to the scientific method; often misuses scientific language. |
| Peer review | Expert evaluation before publication to ensure quality and validity; a key quality‑control mechanism. |

## Question Bank
### Multiple-Choice
1. Q: Which design most reduces expectation bias in a medical trial?
- A. Open trial with no control
- B. Single‑blind without placebo
- C. Double‑blind with placebo control
- D. Case study with historical controls
<details><summary>Answer</summary>C. Double‑blind placebo‑controlled design minimises participant/researcher expectations. ([tga.gov.au](https://www.tga.gov.au/resources/guidance/australian-clinical-trial-handbook?utm_source=openai))</details>

2. Q: A media article claims “Eating ice cream causes sunburn.” Your best first response is to:
- A. Accept it; correlation proves causation
- B. Dismiss it; correlation is always meaningless
- C. Seek the original study to check controls and confounders (e.g., temperature/season)
- D. Assume fraud
<details><summary>Answer</summary>C. Check the primary source for design and confounders; correlation alone is insufficient. ([abs.gov.au](https://www.abs.gov.au/statistics/understanding-statistics/statistical-terms-and-concepts/correlation-and-causation?utm_source=openai))</details>

### Short-Answer
1. Q: Give two indicators a claim is pseudoscientific.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Not falsifiable/testable; misuses scientific jargon to mask lack of evidence; absence of peer‑reviewed support; reliance on testimonials (drawn from definition and IQ4 focus).</details>

2. Q: Briefly explain one benefit and one limitation of peer review.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Benefit: filters poor methods and improves clarity, aiding trust. Limitation: potential bias and capacity constraints with growing volume (IQ5); see COPE guidance on managing bias. ([publicationethics.org](https://publicationethics.org/resources/forum-discussions/bias-peer-review?utm_source=openai))</details>

## Introduction
This module examines how scientific events and research affect public trust; why research is regulated; and how economic, social and political forces shape science. Australian ethical frameworks (NHMRC 2023 National Statement) and organ donation systems (DonateLife) provide contemporary context. ([nhmrc.gov.au](https://www.nhmrc.gov.au/research-policy/ethics/national-statement-ethical-conduct-human-research?utm_source=openai), [donatelife.gov.au](https://www.donatelife.gov.au/?utm_source=openai))

## Inquiry Question 1 – How do science-related events affect society's view of science?
### Concepts
- Investigate past events and their effect on science’s public image.

## Inquiry Question 2 – Why is scientific research regulated?
### Concepts
- Investigate the need for regulation of research.
- Assess ethical issues surrounding current research.
- Investigate international scientific codes of conduct regarding research and practice.
- Evaluate the effectiveness of international regulation in research and practice.

### Definitions (from graph)
- Ethical research (NHMRC core principles): Informed Consent; Beneficence; Justice. HSC example: 2020 Q25b—ethics committee conditions for self‑injection scenario. ([nhmrc.gov.au](https://www.nhmrc.gov.au/research-policy/ethics/national-statement-ethical-conduct-human-research?utm_source=openai))

## Inquiry Question 3 – How do economic, social and political influences affect scientific research?
### Concepts
- Evaluate costs of space exploration relative to social investments.
- Evaluate how scientific research aids economic development and human progress.
- Evaluate impacts of research, devices and applications on world health and wellbeing.
- Analyse impacts of governments and corporations on research (conflicts of interest).
- Evaluate how personal, cultural and socioeconomic perspectives influence research direction.

### Definitions (from graph)
- Conflict of interest: when private interests (e.g., funding ties) could improperly influence professional judgement. HSC examples: 2022 Q33b corporate funding; 2020 Q32c climate communication conflict.
- Social/political influence: scientific evidence can inform political decisions and shape public opinion. HSC example: 2019 Q30b Franklin River Dam—scientific evidence informing political/legal outcomes. ([peo.gov.au](https://peo.gov.au/understand-our-parliament/history-of-parliament/history-milestones/australian-parliament-history-timeline/events/high-court-rules-on-the-franklin-dam-case?utm_source=openai))

## Question Bank
### Multiple-Choice
1. Q: According to current Australian guidance, which statement is most accurate?
- A. The 2007 National Statement is the current guideline
- B. The 2023 National Statement took effect on 1 Jan 2024 and supersedes the 2007 (updated 2018) version
- C. Ethics review is optional for minimal‑risk human research
- D. Only universities must follow the National Statement
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. NHMRC states the 2023 National Statement is effective from 1 Jan 2024, superseding the 2007/2018 version. ([nhmrc.gov.au](https://www.nhmrc.gov.au/research-policy/ethics/national-statement-ethical-conduct-human-research?utm_source=openai))</details>

2. Q: Which practice most clearly mitigates conflict‑of‑interest risks in research publications?
- A. Using emotive language to persuade readers
- B. Declaring and managing funding relationships per recognised codes of conduct
- C. Only publishing positive results
- D. Submitting to non‑peer‑reviewed outlets for speed
<details><summary>Answer</summary>B. Disclosure and management per the Australian Code/COPE practices. ([nhmrc.gov.au](https://www.nhmrc.gov.au/research-policy/research-integrity/2018-australian-code-responsible-conduct-research?utm_source=openai))</details>

### Short-Answer
1. Q: Give one regulatory/organisational mechanism that supports ethical organ transplantation internationally.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>WHO Guiding Principles (e.g., altruistic donation; transparency; allocation by clinical criteria) provide an ethical framework for jurisdictions. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/publications/i/item/WHO-HTP-EHT-CPR-2010.01?utm_source=openai))</details>

2. Q: Briefly describe how a historic science event improved public trust in science.
<details><summary>Answer</summary>Smallpox eradication (declared 1980) demonstrated the power of coordinated, evidence‑based vaccination, enhancing confidence in science’s societal value. ([who.int](https://www.who.int/health-topics/smallpox?utm_source=openai))</details>
